question: A report by the Committee on Constitutional Affairs (AFCO) reviewing the 2024 European elections contains numerous proposals for reforming EU electoral law. These include calls for a uniform minimum voting age of 16, a mandatory electoral threshold of between 3.5% and 5%, a more binding lead candidate principle and far-reaching meddling in national electoral laws.
It further advocates for the European Parliament to play a more prominent role in appointing the Commission and the expansion of measures to ‘promote democracy’. 1.
How will the Commission ensure that the European Democracy Shield is not misused as a political tool for opinion control and censorship, especially against Eurosceptic or conservative voices?

Why has the Commission remained silent on the fact that voter turnout in many EU countries remains dramatically low – in some cases below 25% – despite the EU’s supposed efforts to strengthen democracy, and does the Commission see this behaviour as a sign of the failure of European-level politics?
How does the Commission justify its ongoing efforts to ‘harmonise’ national electoral law, even though under to Article 223 TFEU this is clearly a matter for the Member States?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.3.2026) The European Democracy Shield1 consists of a wide range of concrete measures to empower, protect, and promote strong and resilient democracies. One fundamental feature of European democracy is that all citizens, as well as political, media or other actors should have the right to freely express their views and opinions.

They should also be able to access and partake information in a reliable and trustworthy information space, free from interference. This is key to exercising democratic rights. Strengthening transparency, accountability and integrity in the information space is therefore an important priority of the European Democracy Shield. The Commission has published a report on the 2024 elections to the European Parliament2.

Among others, it analyses voter turnout in different Member States and highlights some factors which may influence it. The organisation and conduct of elections are the competence of the Member States. Under Article 22 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, the Commission can draw up proposals3 to facilitate the exercise of electoral rights by mobile EU citizens4.

On 24 June 2025, the Council Directive (EU) 2025/1788 laying down detailed arrangements for the exercise of the right to vote and to stand as a candidate in elections to the European Parliament for Union citizens residing in a Member State of which they are not nationals (recast) was adopted. Member States have until June 2027 to transpose the Directive into national laws.

The proposal for a Council Directive laying down detailed arrangements for the exercise of the right to vote and to stand as a candidate in municipal elections by Union citizens residing in a Member State of which they are not nationals (recast) is still under discussion in the Council. 4 EU citizens who have moved to another Member State to work, live or study.
